description: Health, fitness, exercise and performance defined, plus the ten components needed for sport.
content_html:
Health and Fitness: Not the Same Thing

Most people use the words “healthy” and “fit” interchangeably, but in sports science they have precise, separate definitions. Health is defined as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not simply the absence of illness. A person can feel stressed, anxious or socially isolated and still have no diagnosable disease, meaning their health is compromised even if a doctor finds nothing wrong.

Fitness, in contrast, is defined as the ability to meet the demands of the environment. This makes fitness specific to purpose: a sprinter needs explosive power and speed; a marathon runner needs cardiovascular endurance; a goalkeeper needs agility and reaction time. A person who is highly fit for one sport may be relatively unfit for another.

Two further definitions complete the picture. Exercise is any form of physical activity that maintains or improves health and fitness — it is a subset of physical activity that has a deliberate fitness aim. Performance refers to how effectively a person executes a skill or task during physical activity or competition. All four concepts — health, fitness, exercise and performance — are distinct but closely related: regular exercise improves fitness, which supports both health and performance.

Key Fact

Four key definitions: Health = complete physical, mental and social well-being. Fitness = ability to meet demands of the environment. Exercise = physical activity that maintains or improves health/fitness. Performance = how well a person executes a skill in sport. Being fit does not automatically mean being healthy, and vice versa.

Health-Related Components of Fitness

The ten components of fitness are divided into two groups. The health-related components are those most directly linked to a person’s physical health and ability to resist lifestyle diseases. There are five:

Cardiovascular endurance (also called aerobic endurance) is the ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period. Distance runners, rowers and cyclists have very high cardiovascular endurance. Strength is the maximum force a muscle or group of muscles can exert in a single effort against a resistance. A rugby prop in a scrum relies heavily on strength. Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or group of muscles to sustain repeated contractions against a resistance for an extended period — a rower completing a 2,000-metre race or a cyclist climbing a hill over many minutes both need muscular endurance. Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. Gymnasts require extreme flexibility across multiple joints. Body composition is the ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone and organs) in the body. A healthy body composition supports both performance and long-term health.

Skill-Related Components of Fitness

The skill-related components are those that primarily affect the quality of sporting performance rather than general health. There are five:

Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining control. A rugby winger sidestepping a defender or a tennis player changing court position both rely on agility. Balance is the ability to maintain the body’s centre of mass over its base of support, either statically (standing still) or dynamically (moving). A gymnast performing a handstand uses static balance; a surfer uses dynamic balance.

Coordination is the ability to use different body parts together in a smooth, accurate and controlled way. A cricket batsman hitting a ball requires the coordination of eyes, hands and body rotation. Power is the ability to exert maximum muscular force in the shortest possible time — it combines strength and speed. A sprinter leaving the starting blocks and a discus thrower generating release velocity both rely on power. Reaction time is the time taken to detect a stimulus and initiate a response. A swimmer diving off the blocks in response to the starting signal, or a goalkeeper reacting to a penalty kick, both rely on short reaction times.

Finally, speed is the ability to move the body or a limb quickly from one point to another. A 100 m sprinter requires maximum running speed; a fast bowler in cricket needs arm speed to generate ball velocity.

Key Fact

Health-related: cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition. Skill-related: agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed. Most sports require a combination of both groups — a basketball player needs cardiovascular endurance (health-related) and agility and coordination (skill-related).

When a question asks you to link components of fitness to a sport, you must justify the choice. Saying “a footballer needs speed” earns half the marks; saying “a footballer needs speed to chase a through-ball and get to it before the defender” earns full marks. For each component you name, follow the pattern: name the component, identify when in the sport it is needed, and explain how it affects performance. Mark schemes reward the link between the component and the sporting context, not just the component name alone.

A common misconception is that a very fit person is automatically healthy, or that an unhealthy person cannot be fit. The two are related but distinct. An elite gymnast may have excellent flexibility, cardiovascular endurance and body composition (very fit) but suffer from disordered eating or stress-related injury (compromised health). Conversely, a person with a diagnosed chronic condition such as controlled diabetes may score below norms on fitness tests but maintain good mental and social well-being (reasonably healthy). Recognising this distinction is important for exam questions that ask you to compare or contrast the two concepts.
exam_tip_html: On Define questions (2 marks), give the precise definition rather than an everyday description. “Fitness is how fit you are” earns nothing; “Fitness is the ability to meet the demands of the environment” earns the mark. When a question asks you to “explain the importance of a specific component of fitness for a named sport,” use the three-step structure: name the component, say when it is needed in the sport, and explain how having it improves performance. For 6-mark Analyse questions involving components of fitness, selecting two components and fully developing each (with an applied sporting example) will reach a higher band than listing five components without development.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health (complete physical, mental and social well-being) and fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) are distinct concepts; being fit does not automatically mean being healthy.
  • The five health-related components are cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. The five skill-related components are agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed.
  • Matching components to a sport requires justification — name the component, identify when it is used, and explain how it improves performance.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a health-related component of fitness?
A) Agility
B) Coordination
C) Muscular endurance
D) Reaction time

practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for reference to meeting demands; 1 mark for reference to the environment (or specific task / activity). Full definition: the ability to meet the demands of the environment.

practice_questions.text: Describe two skill-related components of fitness that are important for a basketball player.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks across two components. For each component: 1 mark for naming the correct skill-related component (agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time or speed); 1 mark for a relevant description of how it is used in basketball (e.g. agility — changing direction quickly to evade defenders; reaction time — responding rapidly to the ball being passed). Award up to 3 marks total; a fully developed point for one component can earn 2, with 1 for a second basic point.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between health and fitness, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being (1); fitness is the ability to meet the demands of the environment, which is sport/activity specific (1); example showing the distinction — e.g. an elite athlete may be very fit but experiencing poor mental health due to competition stress, so fitness and health do not always coincide (1).

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old long-distance runner wants to improve her overall performance before the county championships. Analyse which components of fitness are most important to her event and explain how they contribute to performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies cardiovascular endurance as the primary component (ability of heart/lungs to supply oxygen during sustained running), links directly to performance (delays onset of fatigue, enables maintenance of pace over distance). Also addresses muscular endurance (leg muscles sustaining repeated contractions over the full race distance), flexibility (stride length and injury prevention), and potentially body composition (lower fat mass reduces load to carry). Each component analysed with a specific link to long-distance running performance. Technically precise, applied throughout.

Secure: Correctly identifies two or three relevant components. Provides sporting link for each. Mostly accurate.

Developing: Names components without full development. Some link to running.

Emerging: Names one component. Basic point only.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of health-related components of fitness compared to skill-related components for a gymnast competing in a floor routine.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For health-related — flexibility is critical for performing extreme joint ranges required by gymnastic positions; muscular endurance is needed for sustained explosive elements throughout the routine; strength underpins all tumbling elements and holds. Against sole focus on health-related — skill-related components are equally or more important: coordination is essential for smooth, controlled multi-joint movements; balance is fundamental for handstands, scales and landing; power is required for tumbling passes. Conclusion: both groups are essential and cannot be separated in gymnastics; the floor routine tests virtually every component. The gymnast who combines exceptional flexibility and strength with elite coordination and balance will outperform one who is strong but uncoordinated. Balanced, applied, concluded.

Secure: Discusses both groups with gymnastic application and a conclusion. Mostly accurate.

Developing: Focuses on one group more than the other. Some application.

Emerging: Names components without evaluation. Limited context.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct definition of health?
options: The ability to meet the demands of the environment
A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
The absence of injury or illness
How well a person performs in sport

knowledge_checks.q: Which component of fitness is defined as the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining control?
The ability to exert maximum muscular force in the shortest possible time, combining strength and speed, is called _____.
Body composition, flexibility, muscular endurance, strength and cardiovascular endurance are all _____ components of fitness.
Match each component of fitness to its definition:
right: The ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to muscles over a sustained period
The time taken to detect a stimulus and begin a response
The range of movement possible at a joint

flashcard_questions.q: What is the definition of health?
flashcard_questions.a: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the definition of fitness?
flashcard_questions.a: The ability to meet the demands of the environment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the definition of exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Any physical activity that maintains or improves health and fitness.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five health-related components of fitness.
flashcard_questions.a: Cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition.
The ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period.
The ability of a muscle to sustain repeated contractions against a resistance for an extended period.
The ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining control.
The ability to exert maximum muscular force in the shortest possible time; strength combined with speed.
The time taken to detect a stimulus and initiate a response.
The ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone and organs) in the body.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one sporting example where coordination is the most critical component of fitness.
flashcard_questions.a: Cricket batting — coordinating eyes, hands and body rotation to strike the ball.
The ability to maintain the body's centre of mass over its base of support.

glossary_terms.definition: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
The ability to meet the demands of the environment.
Any form of physical activity that maintains or improves health and fitness.
How well a person executes a skill or task in physical activity or sport.
Components of fitness directly linked to overall health status, including cardiovascular endurance, strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Components of fitness that contribute to sporting skill and performance rather than general health, including agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed.
The ability to change body position quickly and accurately while maintaining control.
The ability to maintain the body's centre of mass over its base of support.
The smooth, accurate and controlled movement of different body parts together.
The ability to exert maximum muscular force in the shortest possible time; a combination of strength and speed.
The time taken to detect a stimulus and initiate a response.
The ability to move the body or a body part quickly from one point to another.
